Machine learning model predicts flight delays from weather data

Published 2026-10-05 19:30 UTC

Researchers at a European university say they have built a machine learning model that predicts flight delays from weather data more accurately than the estimates airlines give passengers. In tests on two years of departures from twelve busy airports, the model's delay predictions were on average 18 minutes closer to the actual departure time than airline estimates published two hours before scheduled departure.

The model combines weather forecasts at the departure and arrival airports with information about the aircraft's previous legs, runway configuration and typical congestion at that time of day. The researchers found that delays often begin hours earlier at another airport, when a thunderstorm slows arrivals and the same aircraft is scheduled for several more flights that day.

Airlines already use their own forecasting tools, but their public estimates tend to be cautious. The study's authors say carriers have an incentive to avoid announcing long delays early, because passengers may rebook with a competitor or the delay may shrink. The model has no such incentive and simply tries to predict when the aircraft will actually leave the gate.

The researchers also measured where the model struggles. It performs poorly when delays are caused by crew shortages, maintenance problems or air traffic control strikes, none of which appear in the weather data. Winter storms are easier to predict than summer thunderstorms, which develop quickly and are hard to forecast precisely.

The team has released its code and a cleaned version of the dataset so other researchers can test the approach. They hope airports will use similar models to plan gate assignments and ground crews, and they say a public version could help travelers decide whether to leave for the airport early or wait at home.

Independent experts said the results were promising but cautioned that the study covered only European airports with good weather data. Performance at smaller airports, where forecasts are less detailed, may be weaker.
